title: business words I never use
content:
from my podcast: botanical studies of internet magic
listen on spotify / listen on apple

when thinking (or talking) about my business, there's at least twenty words I don't use -- many of them super basic, like "marketing," "sales," "landing page," "launch," or "productivity" ... even "goals." I've rewritten my own creative business dictionary -- because language shapes our relationship to our worlds. I'll list the words, and tell you what words I use instead.

rewriting my language helps me recreate my entire paradigm -- to create a business that values agency over manipulation, ecosystem webs over linear metrics -- and grow a system that I actually love, and want to live in.

Recently, I realized that when I'm talking about my creative business, I have to put air quotes around a lot of the words that I use like marketing and launch and sales pages. Because when I think about those things in my own business, I have other words that I made up for myself. And it takes a long time to sort of explain what those other words are. I'm always doing a sort of translation process in my brain, but I thought I'd make a podcast episode about this because I think the ways in which I've rewritten business language has had a big impact on how I reframe and shape the ways in which I relate to my business.

Language is like the wrapping or packaging around a thing that you do. And if I thought about sharing my work as quote unquote marketing, I will probably never do it. So this episode is about all the words that I don't use to myself in my business and what words I use instead. And I think if you peel back the layers, you'll see that rewriting language is really about shifting a paradigm for how I think about doing business in a way that feels generative, nourishing, and authentic to who I am.

As a caveat, like everything that I share of my personal process, this is such a personal list. It will probably change in the next couple of months. And it's a sort of peek into a map of my brain. I hope that this list will give you some new ideas and also encourage you to think about what words you use, what words you struggle with and how to reframe them. Because I think there's no rules because you make the rules and language is a way of rulemaking.

Okay, so there's more than 21 business words that I rewrote in my head. And therefore concepts that I've reshaped, I've divided them into four categories. Marketing and sales, money and value, metrics and measuring success, and relationship and identity. Let's dive in.

Marketing & Sales

Marketing

I never use the word marketing because it feels super outcome oriented. Like the purpose of marketing is to bring something to a market where I can sell it. It feels like it's to market my work, is to hope that someone will pay attention to me, buy something. Instead, I use the word or the phrase sharing my work. That's it, super simple.

Sharing my work is a practice and process instead of the outcome of someone paying attention to me. Sharing my work is separate from how many clicks I get, how many people read my emails. Sharing just focuses on moving my work from private world to public world. This is something I talk a lot about in my course, Sharing Space Camp. It's sending my work into the void. Whatever happens after I release it into the void does not actually concern me. I mean, it does, but it doesn't concern the practice of sharing my work.

Therefore, because marketing and promotion is just about sharing my work, I don't distinguish between types of sharing. I don't distinguish between sharing art versus sharing a paid offering. Energetically, it's technically the same thing. It's something I made that I put creative energy into. Therefore, technically everything I do is considered quote unquote marketing.


Sales/Selling

Okay, as you might expect, the second word is sales or selling. I really think of sales and selling as sharing my work part two. And I know that in marketing psychology, marketing is about telling people about what you have and they're at the awareness stage, whereas sales is bringing them to the consideration stage in which they debate internally or out loud few whether or not they're going to buy your thing.

To me, I think about selling as simply inviting someone past a gated threshold where they have to buy a key or a ticket to get behind the threshold and the threshold is a price. It's money, it's a container, a boundary that they pass through. And so it's really not that different from marketing in that it's also about passing a threshold.

When you share your work, you bring people in from the digital universal space into your website, which I think of as a house or a world. And then when you sell your work, you're bringing them from your public spaces like your living room or your public gardens into a more private space. So behind a locked door or a gate.

And so because I don't really have the concept of sales or selling other than sharing my work part two, I don't really do sales emails. Like I will never send an email. I mean, never say never, but to this point I have not sent an email whose sole purpose is about selling one thing. I do sell things inside my emails, but because I want each and every email people get from me to feel rich and nourishing and meaningful, like a feast, I don't want an email just to be focused on trying to sell them something. I want it to feel like an offering regardless if they buy something or not.


Landing Page

The third word is landing page or sales page. And I think the word landing feels vague and weird like landing from what? Landing from where? Are people on the internet just floating in the atmosphere until they land onto a page where they could get sucked into your marketing funnel? Yeah, I don't think of it like that.

The word I use instead to replace landing page is invitations page. And the invitations page is akin to the gated threshold or the locked door. There is an intimacy to that invitation. It's showing them a peak of what's behind this door or behind this gated threshold, giving them information, a sense of intrigue, and ultimately giving them agency. The decision rests with them. Do they want to enter? Do they want to respond to this invitation?

And I think it doesn't matter if this invitations page is for a paid offering or a free offering. There's still a sense of crossing a threshold. In the invitations page, I include the heart and essence of this space that I've created for them or this offering that I've imagined for them. And they decide how to respond.

Funnel

The next word is funnel. Applied to either marketing or sales. So marketing funnel, sales funnel. I wrote a post about this a couple of years ago called "Build a Labyrinth, Not a Funnel." My main problem with the word funnel is that it feels kind of slippery and relying on gravity, like pulling people down the funnel.

I prefer language that feels like it gives people more agency and autonomy. So I like to use the word creating a labyrinth, creating a world, creating a breadcrumb trail, like leaving little crumbs or tiny cakes in the forest, giving them a tasting menu that leads to the gated feast if they want more. And at each step of the way, each part of the world, labyrinth or forest, each visitor gets to decide, do I want to continue? Do I want to follow this trail and see where it leads me?

Lead Magnet

The next word is lead magnet. I don't do lead magnets because they feel transactional. I was tempted at the beginning of building my business because it seems like a sort of go-to business strategy, but I never did it because it just felt kind of sticky. Do you really want this ebook? If so, give me your email address.

I want you to give me your email address of your own accord. I think in building any kind of relationship with people, with visitors on the internet, agency and choice and consent is so important. And I don't want any kind of manipulation to be a part of the equation. When someone decides to sign up for my email list.

Launch

The last word of this category of marketing and sales is the word launch. I find myself using the word launch, even though I really hate this word because launch assumes that there's a right way to share an offering. A launch cycle or a launch sequence must happen in these exact steps.

To me, launching just takes too much energy. It's like launching a rocket into outer space. It feels pretty phallic. And once you spend all this energy launching, afterwards you just feel tired or I feel really tired.

So instead I like to use the word release, kind of like releasing wild animals into the forest, into the ecosystem or birthing something and seeing what happens. I think releasing expectations, releasing creations, there's an act of surrender inherent in it.

One of my rules for launching or releasing a new offering into the world is energy generativity. So whatever energy I spend to release this offering, I want that energy to serve me in the future. This is partially why I don't send sales emails. And instead my release strategy is usually to create more creative projects around the core offering because they will continue to exist over time and they won't disappear as a single email in your inbox.

VALUE AND MONEY

The next category I wanna talk about is the language of value and money.

Income/Expenses

The first word is income. I don't really like using the word income even though it feels so basic. I use the word inflow, like what is the flow that's coming in and what is the flow that's going out so expenses. Even in my tax spreadsheet, I renamed the tabs inflow and outflow because inherent in that language is seeing money as circulation, as a cycle, as a circle of being inflow or conversation with the world. Creating resources and giving resources.

Products and Services

The next word is products and services. Personally, in my head, I prefer to use the word offering. I like the vagueness of the word offering. It's like you make offerings on the altar, you offer an idea, an opinion, a thought.

The word offering applies to something that is both public, free and paid because I think of the energy as the same. Part of the fundamental paradigm of how I create for my business is to think of my paid offerings with the same energy as my creative projects that are free and public.

When I think of everything as an offering, I remove the pressure to prove that any particular offering is worthy of your time, attention and money. And yes, technically I do sell services and products, but I want all my services and products to carry the intentionality and sacredness of an offering.

Value Proposition

The next word is value proposition. I remember when I was starting my business, this word gave me a lot of headaches. Trying to figure out what is a value proposition, it was in every business book or worksheet that I was pushing myself to work through. I think this word creates pressure, pressure to prove that something is worthy of your time, attention, money.

And instead, when I'm thinking about what to write on my landing/invitations page, I mostly start by writing about why this matters to me and my intentions for creating this for you and how I hope it can help you. So a value proposition is really a statement of intention. And that's why having absolute clarity on the heart of your offering, why you're creating something and releasing it to the world, that is the best juice for not even persuasion, but standing by the value of what you have to give.

ROI

The last word in this category is ROI. ROI is a very triggering word for me because I remember at the early stages of starting my business, my dad who has an MBA often asked me about the ROI of my efforts. Over the last many years, I realized that ROI is a difficult word, at least when you're an artist building a business because my paradigm is about interconnectivity. Whereas ROI assumes a direct A to B one-to-one relationship when the energy that I put into something travels along the ecosystem webs over time.

And so instead of saying or measuring the ROI of something, I'll just say this thing works really well for me. So for example, my ROI of sending a newsletter or creating a podcast episode is higher than writing a piece on my website. And yet I would never think of it like that. I think of it as more people listen to a single podcast episode than they read a single post.

To some people, maybe ROI can feel like a really clarifying concept that can help them prioritize. But for me, I don't measure ROI because the moment that I do, it can make something feel like an obligation.

I think it's important to be really specific about what is the thing that you want to work on, improve or evolve. And instead I focus on the channels. If I have multiple channels for sharing my work, how do I make the channels have a greater sense of flow? Which channels feel most strategic or effective or alive to focus on in this moment?

And as a side note, something that feels strategic may not be the thing that feels most exciting. Usually excitement and energy for me wins over strategic thinking because strategy doesn't really work without the inspiration and energy to execute it.

Metrics & Measuring Success

The third category is language that measures success and metrics.

Goals

The first word I'll say is the word goals. I have definitely felt traumatized by being too much of an ambitious goal setter. Goals feels too linear overall. It's like either you score a goal or you don't. Instead, I like to use the word expeditions, adventures, quests, to think about the process of pursuing a goal as a journey through unknown territory.

And maybe you'll make an itinerary, maybe you'll have milestones for tracking progress. Maybe there's a linearity within the bigger journey, but there's still an element of spontaneity and discovery that's inherent to an expedition or adventure. When I frame it in that way, I'm just more excited to work on my goals.


Productive

The second word is productive. Trust me, there were many years where I used to say, I had a productive day as a sign of success for that day. I was such a productivity addict during that time. You can listen to a previous podcast episode, episode number 17, transcendence of a productivity addict.

I'm really careful about the word productive because I don't want to insinuate that being productive makes any day more worthy or higher in value than a "unproductive day." When I'm speaking to myself or my clients or students, I use the word inflow, what felt inflow this week or easeful or satisfying or fulfilling just to start and disconnect the conditioning and programming that we are here to produce and to be laborious machines of productivity.

For example, some days having a whole day to wander in a park can generate so many new ideas, but what I call that productive, I'm not sure. So I try not to use this word at all.

Optimize

The next word is optimize. The word optimize is just a little too vague. Optimize for what? I mean, usually it's a metric, like more traffic, more subscribers, more sales, but the problem I have with this word is that optimize assumes that more is better, but more isn't always better. I think higher quality is better, deeper connection is better.

Instead of optimize, I usually use the word evolve, and I think about the nature of this evolution. How do I want to evolve it? What am I hoping for from this evolution? And getting really specific on that.

SEO

The next word is SEO, search engine optimization. I'll have a mini brag in this moment, which is I have pretty good SEO, but I never spend more than a couple of seconds thinking about SEO. And the way that I think about SEO is how do I make my work more findable in the library of the internet?

So thinking of the internet as a giant infinite library, and there's a robot moving around the library, finding the books or fragments of papers that people are looking for using keywords. And sometimes these words are like very basic words. It's the first word that comes to mind when you put your fingers over a keyboard or when you speak a word into the search engine.

So I think of SEO as mostly what language makes this piece recognizable and understandable. What are some words that connect this creation that I've made to the right people? And if I were to build a business from scratch that relied on SEO, the secret that I would say is that the more specific, the better.

Open Rates

The next word is open rates. I don't use this word because I don't look at my analytics for my newsletter and just thinking about the word open rates stresses me out because open rates exist to measure the success or failure of an email title. And I don't want to optimize that. I don't want to overthink that. So I just turn off open rates.

Conversion Rates

The last word is conversion rates. Similar to open rates, I can see where a conversion rate could be useful to measure. Like if you have a thousand people visit this page and only 10 of them by, then your conversion rate is 1%. Thinking about conversion rates can help you find clarity on whether you need to focus on having more people visit this page or having a more compelling, evocative landing slash invitations page.

This is to say, I know that conversion rates are useful business concepts to measure and think about. It's just that I personally don't. If a resource that I've created, if an offering I created isn't selling as well as I would like it to, I would think about the reason why. And usually the reason why is related to how it's connected or disconnected from the rest of my ecosystem. Are there clear pathways and breadcrumb trails? Is it specific enough? Nothing I create exists in isolation.

Conversion rate exists to measure the success of one thing, like one sales page or one email. And I don't use this terminology because I prefer to think about the entire ecosystem. As a whole, instead of focusing on how can I make this page convert more sales, I think about what does this page need to be more truthful of the essence of the offering that I've created.

Relationship & Identity

The last category is words that describe relationship and identity. So how I relate to myself and others who come into my ecosystem.

Customer Persona/Avatar

The first word that I don't use is customer persona or customer avatar. I took some marketing seminars when I worked my first job in which they encourage you to imagine who it is that you're selling to and to create several different customer personas.

To me, personas or avatars feel just too fake and cardboardy. So instead of imagining a specific demographic or type of person, I prefer to imagine a real person, like someone in my community, a previous student or client that I've worked with or a friend. And I imagine writing that invitation page or email to them.

For me, writing one-to-one has always been more effective in getting me in the mood. I can be more specific and universal when I think about one real person because a real person is multidimensional. A real person has depth and complexity and so many different facets that feel chaotic and messied and don't always make sense. If I write to that real person, I'm more likely to attract people into my world who are drawn to that messiness and complexity and depth. And those are the kinds of people that I want in my world.

Pitch

The next word is pitch, as in the verb, to pitch something or to send an email pitch. I don't have another word for this because I don't pitch anything or anyone pretty much ever. I don't send cold emails hoping for a result.

I'm pretty triggered by the word elevator pitch because it creates so much pressure. Like you have to distill what it is that you have or offer in like three minutes, which is not to say that I don't find value in distillation and sharing the essence of whatever it is that I've created or what it is that I do, but in part because in human design, I'm a projector. So my strategy is to wait for people to come to me and not to pitch someone else, but also because I think this word pitch creates anxiety. So I prefer to think of it as distillation, looking for the heart, the core of what it is that you're offering.

Branding

The next word is branding. I do branding as a creative service. I've done branding for many years, but I don't even like to call it branding because the word branding sounds so external. It sounds like packaging, like how something looks to another person. There's an artifice about branding and the way in which I do branding and I hesitate to even call it branding is to start with the essence.

So to start with the heart, the soul, the internal, almost subliminal truth of what something is. It's deep identity work and it's deep distillation work. It's like finding the notes of a perfume. It's expressing who you are clearly in visual language and words.

So the word that I use to describe branding is more something like essence distillation. And for me, world building is the creative practice that encompasses branding and identity work. Along with marketing and sales and everything else.

Audience

The last word that I'll leave you with, the word that I don't like to use is audience. It's hard not to use this word. I wrote about it in a post called Build a World, Not an Audience. When I think of the word audience, it kind of makes me freeze up when I imagine an audience sitting in chairs in an auditorium or like showing up, it gets me a little bit stage Friday. And maybe this is just me feeling a bit shy in front of an audience.

I think there is truthfully a distinction between an audience and a community. And it's about the relationship. The community feels more bi-directional. There's an ongoing conversation. Whereas an audience feels a bit more receptive.

So instead of audience, in my head, I think of my audience as my visitors to my world, my listeners, my readers, the recipients of my letters, internet strangers and stranger friends. And friends defined in a abstract, more philosophical term, even if I don't know you, I assume that the reason you're here is because something about my work resonates with you that in some dimension, in some world, we could be friends.

closing notes

That concludes my list of over 21 words that I don't use in my business and have reinvented or translated for myself, at least when speaking to myself in my own head. Thank you for listening to this ongoing dictionary of my business language.

I think of language as very much alive. So by the time you listen to this in the future, it's likely that my own language and ways of relating to these words and concepts will already have shifted. By no means, again, is this list prescriptive. If anything, many of these words and concepts took me years to clarify and sense into the shape of. And many of them, I tried out different words for the same concept.

It feels a little bit like collecting the perfect seashell and you don't quite know what word you're looking for until you find that word that feels just perfect. And other words are changing and maybe you release them back into the sea.

I invite you to notice the words you use around your business, which words feel sticky or restrictive or triggering or anxiety-dosing or stressful, even a little bit. Can you soften around those words? Can you search for another word, another shape or container that can provide another way of relating to these business practices and processes? Because ultimately, your business is the sum of your way of relating to it. So you get to decide how you do it and what words you use to cultivate and tend to that relationship.
